title.text: Five small builds, from linear regression to attention, written from first principles

objects.text: Can five small builds, written from first principles, reproduce the core of what runs inside modern AI?

Mathematics for AI and Machine Learning  |  Session 18 of 18  |  Course project
KLAi Professional Learning  |  Jotham Martin Wambi

slides.notes:
Welcome to the last session. For seventeen sessions you collected tools: vectors, matrices, eigenvalues, gradients, probability, likelihood, entropy. Today you use them in five small builds. Four of them use only what you already know. The fifth, attention, is new: every part of it is familiar, and how the parts fit together is what you learn today.

The question for today is this: Can five small builds, written from first principles, reproduce the core of what runs inside modern AI? Keep it in mind. At the end of the session we come back to it and see how much more you can say.

title.text: Today in one view: what you will leave with

objects.text: By the end of today you can
Build linear regression (normal equation and gradient descent) and logistic regression (gradient descent) with numpy
Build PCA from the covariance eigen-decomposition, and a 2-4-1 neural network with backpropagation (take-home)
Learn attention as a ladder of known steps, build it for three tokens, and see OK on the self-checks of your project

slides.notes:
By the end of today you can build five things from first principles. Linear regression, with the normal equation and with gradient descent. Logistic regression, with gradient descent. PCA, from the eigen-decomposition of the covariance matrix. A small neural network, two inputs, four hidden units and one output, with backpropagation, which is the take-home build.

And scaled dot-product attention for three tokens, which is new today and gets the most time. In the notebook the text you type as a student ID makes your own personal data, and automatic self-checks show OK or NOT YET for each build. There are no marks. The project is yours to keep.

title.text:
Your two hours: a guided tour,
attention, then your project

objects.alt: The two hours in parts, in minutes

objects.text: The tour first. Then your project, with self-checks and no marks. Then AI.

slides.notes:
Today is the last session. Ten minutes of recall from Session 17. Thirty-five minutes of concepts: a quick tour of four builds you already have the maths for, then most of the time on attention, which is new. A ten minute break. Then forty-five minutes on your project: aim for Builds 1, 2, 3 and 5 in class, with Build 4 at home.

The project is the notebook, which you build with your own personal data and keep. Nothing is marked: the checks only show you what works. The spreadsheet is a guided version with the same five builds. We finish with where this appears in AI, what to learn next, and saving your work.

title.text: Three questions from last time

runs.text: 1.  How are cross-entropy, entropy and KL divergence related?
2.  What is the gradient of softmax with cross-entropy with respect to the logits?
3.  What does a perplexity of 5 mean?

objects.text: Answer aloud first. Then we check together.

slides.notes:
Three quick questions from Session 17. Answer aloud first, and then we check together. It is a warm-up to bring last time back.

Question one. How are cross-entropy, entropy and KL divergence related? Take a moment.

A good answer is this. Cross-entropy = entropy + KL divergence. The entropy is fixed by the data, so lowering the cross-entropy lowers the KL divergence.

Question two. What is the gradient of softmax with cross-entropy with respect to the logits? Say it to yourself first.

A good answer is this. The prediction minus the target: p - y.

Question three. What does a perplexity of 5 mean? Think about your own task as you answer.

A good answer is this. The model is as unsure as if it chose among about five equally likely words at each step.

If an answer was missing, do not worry. Your notes from last class have it. Now to today.

title.text: Answers to the three questions from Session 17

rows.text: How are cross-entropy, entropy and KL divergence related?
Cross-entropy = entropy + KL divergence. The entropy is fixed by the data, so lowering the cross-entropy lowers the KL divergence.
What is the gradient of softmax with cross-entropy with respect to the logits?
The prediction minus the target: p - y.
What does a perplexity of 5 mean?
The model is as unsure as if it chose among about five equally likely words at each step.

objects.text: All three come back today: p - y trains Builds 2 and 4, and the softmax is inside attention.

slides.notes:
Cross-entropy equals entropy plus KL divergence, and because the entropy is fixed by the data, lowering the cross-entropy lowers the KL. The gradient of softmax with cross-entropy with respect to the logits is the prediction minus the target, and Session 17 showed the same form for a sigmoid with binary cross-entropy.

A perplexity of five means the model is as unsure as if it chose among about five equally likely words. Today the second answer trains two of our builds, and the softmax sits inside attention.

title.text: Words we use today

rows.text: A model that passes a straight-line score through the sigmoid to give a probability between 0 and 1.
A direction of largest spread in the data: an eigenvector of the covariance matrix.
The chain rule applied backwards through a network to get the gradient of the loss for every weight.
The three vectors each token makes in attention: what it looks for, what it offers and what it passes on.
Each token takes a weighted average of the value vectors, with weights from softmax(Q K^T / sqrt(d)).

slides.notes:
Five words for today. I give the plain meaning of each, and we use every one of them before the end of the session.

Logistic regression. A model that passes a straight-line score through the sigmoid to give a probability between 0 and 1.

Principal component. A direction of largest spread in the data: an eigenvector of the covariance matrix.

Backpropagation. The chain rule applied backwards through a network to get the gradient of the loss for every weight.

Query, key, value. The three vectors each token makes in attention: what it looks for, what it offers and what it passes on.

Attention. Each token takes a weighted average of the value vectors, with weights from softmax(Q K^T / sqrt(d)).

The network starts from these weights: a four by two matrix W one, a zero bias b one, four output weights W two and an output bias of 0.1. The four XOR rows have targets zero, one, one, zero. For attention, X has one row per token, and three small matrices make the queries, keys and values.

title.text:
Build 1: linear regression has a
direct solution and an iterative one

objects.alt: Build 1: linear regression has a direct solution and an iterative one

rows.text: The design matrix: a column of ones, then x.
The weights: the intercept b (it multiplies the ones), then the slope w1.

objects.text: At eta 0.02, 100 steps give (0.714, 1.075); about 5,000 steps reach (1.12, 0.98). MSE 0.0213.

slides.notes:
Build one is the line fit of Session 4, y-hat equals b plus w one x, in matrix form. X has a column of ones so that the first weight is the intercept b. The normal equation solves least squares in one line: w equals the inverse of X transpose X, times X transpose y.

Gradient descent with learning rate eta reaches the same answer in small steps, but not quickly. After a hundred steps it is at 0.714 and 1.075. The slope settles early and the intercept catches up slowly, so it takes about five thousand steps to reach 1.12 and 0.98.

The mean squared error is 0.0213. Seven hours is outside the data, so the prediction of 7.98 kilowatt-hours is an extrapolation.

title.text: Build 1 in a picture: the fitted line and its residuals

objects.alt: Build 1 in a picture: the fitted line and its residuals

objects.text: The line is y-hat = 1.12 plus 0.98 x. The red segments are the residuals.

runs.text: Illustrative data: x = 1 to 6 hours, y = 2.2, 2.9, 4.1, 5.2, 5.8, 7.1 kWh.
The normal equation and enough gradient steps give the same line.

slides.notes:
Six points, and the least squares line with intercept 1.12 and slope 0.98. The red segments are the residuals, the gaps between the points and the line. Least squares chooses the line that makes the sum of their squares as small as possible. In Session 16 you saw that this is also maximum likelihood under Gaussian noise.

The data are illustrative. Which point has the largest residual?

title.text:
Logistic regression turns a straight-line
score into a probability with the sigmoid

objects.alt: Logistic regression turns a straight-line score into a probability with the sigmoid

objects.text: Logistic regression: score = b plus w1 x, then p = sigmoid(score), the probability of class 1.

runs.text: The sigmoid of Session 11 squeezes any score into 0 to 1.
Trained on the 8 students: p = 0.5 at 4.5 hours. Predict "pass" above it.

slides.notes:
Logistic regression is a named model you have not met yet, but every part is familiar. Take a straight-line score, b plus w one times x, as in Build 1. Pass it through the sigmoid of Session 11, which squeezes any number into the range zero to one.

The result is read as the probability of passing. The red curve is the model after training on our eight students. The dots at the top passed and the dots at the bottom failed. The curve crosses one half at 4.5 hours, which is where the prediction switches from fail to pass.

title.text:
Build 2: logistic regression is trained by
gradient descent on the cross-entropy

objects.alt: Build 2: logistic regression is trained by gradient descent on the cross-entropy

objects.text: After 5 steps: w = (-0.0509, 0.1494), loss 0.623. Data: 8 students (see the data slide).

slides.notes:
The loss is the binary cross-entropy from Session 16. Its gradient with respect to the score is p minus y. Session 17 showed this two-class form: a sigmoid is a two-class softmax. Averaged over the rows and multiplied by the inputs, that gives the gradient for b and w one.

Starting from zero weights every probability is one half and the loss is 0.693. After five steps with a learning rate of 0.1 the weights are -0.0509 and 0.1494, and the loss has fallen to 0.623. The data are eight illustrative students: hours of study and pass or fail.

title.text:
Build 2 by hand: the loss falls at every
one of the first five gradient steps

objects.text: Learning rate 0.1. Step 0 is the start. The workbook has the same table.

slides.notes:
Step zero is the start, with both weights at zero and a loss of 0.6931. At step one the intercept stays at zero, because half the students passed and the average of p minus y is zero, but the slope moves up. The loss falls at every step, to 0.6232 after five.

In the lab you let it run for thousands of steps, and in the workbook you fill this same table with formulas. With a learning rate of two the steps would overshoot and the loss would jump around.

title.text:
Build 3: PCA finds the direction
of largest spread in the data

objects.alt: Build 3: PCA finds the direction of largest spread in the data

objects.text: The red line is the first principal component. It holds 96.3 percent of the variance.

runs.text: Eigenvalues of the sample covariance matrix: 1.284 and 0.049.
First component: (0.678, 0.735).

slides.notes:
Build three is PCA, principal component analysis, from Sessions 5 and 6. Ten illustrative points in two dimensions. The two columns rise together, so the spread is mostly along one diagonal direction, the red line. That direction is the first principal component. The sample covariance matrix has two eigenvalues, 1.284 and 0.049, so the first component holds 96.3 percent of the total variance.

If we keep only the position of each point along that line, one number instead of two, we lose very little.

title.text:
PCA as formulas: centre, form the
covariance, find its eigenvectors, project

objects.alt: PCA as formulas: centre, form the covariance, find its eigenvectors, project

rows.text: The data with each column centred on its mean.
An eigenvalue: the variance along its eigenvector.
The eigenvector with the largest eigenvalue: the first component.
Sample data divide by n - 1 (Session 5, np.cov).

objects.text: Dividing by n instead (ddof = 0) gives 1.156 and 0.044: the same eigenvectors and the same 96.3 percent share.

slides.notes:
First centre each column on its mean. The ten points are a sample, so the covariance matrix is X c transpose times X c divided by n minus one, as in Session 5 and as np.cov does. Its eigenvectors are the principal components, and each eigenvalue is the variance along its eigenvector.

The largest eigenvalue is 1.284, with eigenvector 0.678 and 0.735. The score of a point is its centred row times that eigenvector. Some libraries divide by n. The eigenvalues are then a little smaller, but the eigenvectors and the share of variance do not change.

title.text:
XOR: no single straight line separates
the two classes, but two lines can

objects.alt: XOR: no single straight line separates the two classes, but two lines can

objects.text: XOR: 1 (gold) when exactly one input is 1, else 0 (white).

slides.notes:
XOR, short for exclusive or, answers one when exactly one of its two inputs is one. Put the four input pairs on a square and colour them: gold for one, white for zero. The gold points sit on one diagonal and the white points on the other. On the left, try any straight line.

It always leaves a gold and a white point on the same side, so logistic regression on the two inputs cannot get all four right. On the right, two lines do the job: gold sits between them. A hidden layer can learn two such lines as new features, and the output then combines them. That is why Build 4 has a hidden layer.

title.text:
Build 4: a 2-4-1 network has two layers
of weights, and the error flows back

objects.alt: Build 4: a 2-4-1 network has two layers of weights, and the error flows back

objects.text: Two inputs, four hidden units, one output. The task is XOR.

runs.text: Forward: h = tanh(W1 x + b1), then p = sigmoid(W2 h + b2).
tanh (Session 11): from -1 to 1, slope 1 - h^2.
Backward: the chain rule passes the error back.

slides.notes:
Build four is a small neural network, two inputs, four hidden units and one output, trained on XOR. The forward pass computes the hidden activations with tanh, which you met in Session 11: an S-shaped curve like the sigmoid, but running from minus one to one, with slope one minus h squared.

Then a sigmoid gives the output probability. The backward pass is backpropagation, the chain rule from Session 9 applied from the output back to the first layer. With a sigmoid output and binary cross-entropy, the first backward quantity is p minus y. Build 4 is the take-home build, with the backward pass scaffolded.

title.text:
Backpropagation for the 2-4-1
network, in matrix algebra

objects.alt: Backpropagation for the 2-4-1 network, in matrix algebra

rows.text: The error signal at the output: p - y for a sigmoid with binary cross-entropy (Session 17).
The error signal arriving at each hidden unit.
The slope of tanh at each hidden unit (Session 11).

objects.text: Update with learning rate eta: each weight matrix and bias becomes W - eta × its gradient.

slides.notes:
The forward pass and the loss are on top. Below, the first backward line says the error signal at the output, delta, is p minus y, the two-class form from Session 17. The gradient for the second weight matrix is delta times the hidden activations, and the gradient for its bias is delta.

The error signal then flows back through the second matrix and is multiplied entry by entry by one minus h squared, the slope of tanh. That gives delta h at the hidden layer, and the gradient for the first weight matrix is delta h times the input. Each weight matrix and bias is then updated by subtracting the learning rate times its gradient.

slides.notes:
Put numbers in. The input is one and two, the target is one. With the starting weights the four hidden activations are -0.100, 0.947, 0.197 and -0.935. The output probability is 0.3888, so the loss is 0.9446. The error signal delta is p minus y, -0.6112. The gradient for the output weights is delta times h.

With a learning rate of 0.5 the first output weight moves from 0.3 to 0.270. The first row of the gradient of W1 is -0.182 and -0.363. In every row of that gradient the second entry is twice the first, because the second input is 2. The workbook has this exact example in cells.

title.text:
After 5,000 gradient steps the toy
network solves XOR (guided example)

objects.text: The loss falls from 0.706 to 0.0008 nats. Learning rate 0.5.

slides.notes:
Before training all four outputs are close to one half, between 0.38 and 0.53, and the loss is 0.706. After five thousand steps of gradient descent the outputs are near zero for the first and last inputs and near one for the middle two, and the loss is 0.0008.

The network has learned XOR, which no single straight line can do. In the notebook the self-checks compare your backward function with a numeric gradient, on your own data.

title.text:
Attention is new today: a ladder
of five steps you already know

objects.alt: Attention is new today: a ladder of five steps you already know

objects.text: Each token asks a question (query), every token offers a label (key) and a message (value).

runs.text: New today: q, k, v and how the steps fit together.
Known: dot products, scaling, softmax, matrix products.
Red numbers: token 1 of the example.

slides.notes:
Attention is new, so we build it as a ladder. The first rung is the new idea. Each token makes three vectors from its embedding: a query, what it is looking for; a key, what it offers to be found by; and a value, the message it passes on.

The other four rungs are tools you have. A dot product from Session 2 scores how well a query matches each key. Dividing by the square root of d k keeps the spread of the scores near one. The softmax of Sessions 12 and 17 turns the scores into weights.

A matrix product from Session 3 takes the weighted average of the values. The red numbers follow token one through every rung.

title.text: By hand: attention for token 1, rung by rung

objects.text: Scores
Scale
Softmax
Average

slides.notes:
Follow token one by hand. Its query is one and zero. The dot products with the three keys are one, zero and one, so token one matches tokens one and three equally. Divide by the square root of two and the scores are 0.707, zero and 0.707. The softmax takes e to each: 2.028, one and 2.028, which add to 5.056.

The weights are 0.401, 0.198 and 0.401, and they add to one. Finally mix the three value vectors with those weights. The output for token one is 0.802 and 1.198: a blend of what the tokens it attends to have to say.

title.text:
Why divide by the square root of d: dot products
of long vectors grow, and the softmax saturates

objects.alt: Why divide by the square root of d: dot products of long vectors grow, and the softmax saturates

objects.text: If the entries of q and k are independent with mean 0 and standard deviation 1, then q . k has mean 0 and standard deviation sqrt(d).

runs.text: Saturate: when scores are large, the softmax puts almost all the weight on one token (nearly one-hot) and its gradient is tiny.
Dividing by sqrt(d_k) keeps the standard deviation near 1. The notebook simulates 2,000 pairs.

slides.notes:
Take two random vectors of length 64, whose entries are independent with mean zero and standard deviation one, as in Session 13. Their dot product is a sum of 64 independent terms, each with variance one, so its variance is 64 and its standard deviation is 8. A simulation of two thousand pairs gives 8.0.

Scores that large make the softmax saturate: almost all the weight goes to one token, and in that region the gradient is tiny, so training stalls. Dividing by the square root of d brings the standard deviation back to about one. This is the reason given in the original paper.

title.text:
Build 5: all three tokens at once,
as a grid of attention weights

objects.alt: Build 5: all three tokens at once, as a grid of attention weights

objects.text: Each row of weights adds to 1. The output is the weights times the value vectors.

slides.notes:
Do the same for every token at once and you get a grid. Each row is one token asking, each column one token being read. Darker gold means a larger weight, and each row adds to one because the softmax runs along the row. Token one is the row you worked by hand.

Token three, in the last row, reads 31 percent from token one, 7 from token two and 62 from itself. On the right, each output is the weighted average of the value vectors. The numbers are made up to show the arithmetic.

title.text:
The whole ladder in one
formula, as published in 2017

objects.alt: The whole ladder in one formula, as published in 2017

rows.text: One row per token: its embedding.
Make queries, keys, values. Learned in a real model.
All query-key dot products at once.
Key length; applied along each row.

objects.text: Vaswani et al. (2017). The W matrices are stored one column per output number, so they multiply on the right as they are.

slides.notes:
This is scaled dot-product attention as Vaswani and colleagues published it in 2017, and every piece is a rung of the ladder. X times the three weight matrices gives the queries, keys and values. Q times K transpose computes every dot product at once, one row per query.

Dividing by the square root of d k is the scaling rung, the softmax runs along each row, and multiplying by V takes the weighted averages. One note on shapes: these weight matrices are stored with one column per output number, as the paper writes them, so they multiply on the right without a transpose.

title.text:
By hand: scaled scores, weights and
output for three tokens (d_k = 2)

objects.text: Illustrative. Scores = Q K^T / sqrt(2). Weights = softmax of each row. Output = weights times V.

slides.notes: The full table. Row one is the token you worked by hand: scaled scores 0.707, 0.000 and 0.707, weights 0.401, 0.198 and 0.401, and output 0.802 and 1.198. Token three has the largest score for itself, 2.828, so it gives itself the largest weight, 0.620. In the workbook the softmax is built in cells with the stable trick of subtracting the row maximum.

title.text: Three slips that the self-checks will catch

objects.text: The slip

runs.text: No column of ones, so no intercept.
PCA without centring the data first.
Softmax along the wrong axis, or no sqrt(d_k).

objects.text: The fix

runs.text: Add the column of ones to X.
Subtract each column mean first.
Softmax along each row; divide scores by sqrt(d_k).

objects.text: Each check names its build, so read the name first.

slides.notes:
Three slips that the checks will catch. In linear regression, forgetting the column of ones means there is no intercept. In PCA, forgetting to centre the data means the covariance is wrong. In attention, applying the softmax down the columns gives rows of weights that do not add to one, and forgetting the square root of d changes every weight.

When a check fails, its name tells you which build to look at. Which of these would you have made?

title.text:
Where this appears in AI: attention is the core
step of every layer of a published transformer

objects.alt: Where this appears in AI: attention is the core step of every layer of a published transformer

objects.text: Published research describes transformer language models as many repeated layers of attention and feed-forward steps.

runs.text: Feed-forward layer: a small network like Build 4 applied to each token. Nonlinearity: a curved function such as tanh between the matrices.
Open models such as Llama add a causal mask: a token cannot read later tokens.

slides.notes:
Published research describes how transformer language models are built. Text becomes tokens and embeddings. Then come many repeated layers. Each layer has an attention step, the core of your build five, and a feed-forward layer: two weight matrices with a nonlinearity, a curved function like tanh, between them, applied to each token like a small Build 4.

At the top a softmax gives next-token probabilities, and training minimises the cross-entropy. Open models such as Llama use the same core formula with a causal mask, which stops a token from reading later tokens. The designs of ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude are not published, so I describe only the published framework.

title.text:
Where this appears in AI: the
five builds in published models

rows.text: Every layer multiplies by a weight matrix. Its weights are found by gradient descent rather than a direct formula, usually with a cross-entropy loss rather than squared error.
The last step of a classifier is a softmax of linear scores, trained with cross-entropy. This many-class version is called softmax regression.
Used to inspect and compress embeddings. LoRA (Hu et al., 2021) learns a low-rank update to a weight matrix, the same low-rank idea.
Backpropagation runs in every training step of published models.
The core step of the transformer, repeated in every layer.

objects.text: Phrased as published research describes. No claim about the internals of any closed product.

slides.notes:
Every layer of a language model multiplies by a weight matrix, a linear map like build one, though its weights are found by gradient descent rather than a direct formula, and usually with a cross-entropy loss. The last step of a classifier is a softmax of linear scores, trained with cross-entropy, which is called softmax regression, the many-class version of build two.

PCA is a way to inspect and compress embeddings, and LoRA learns a low-rank update to a weight matrix. Backpropagation runs in every training step. Attention is the core step of the transformer. I phrase all of this as published research describes it, with no claim about closed products.

title.text:
Exit check: three questions
and their short answers

rows.text: What does each row of the attention weights add up to, and why?
To 1, because a softmax is applied along each row.
Why is the attention score divided by the square root of d_k?
Large dot products make the softmax saturate: almost all the weight goes to one token and the gradient is tiny. The scaling keeps the standard deviation near 1.
In PCA, which eigenvector is the first principal component?
The one with the largest eigenvalue, the direction of largest variance.

objects.text: Answer each in one sentence before you read the right-hand column.

slides.notes:
Three questions to finish. One, each row of the attention weights adds up to one, because a softmax is applied along each row. Two, the score is divided by the square root of d k because large dot products make the softmax saturate, with almost all the weight on one token and a tiny gradient, and the scaling keeps their standard deviation near one.

Three, in PCA the first principal component is the eigenvector with the largest eigenvalue. Cover the right-hand column and answer aloud first.
